cards.q: What must every postmortem end with?
cards.a: At least one concrete guardrail (test, alert, contract, or process change) with an owner and due date.

cards.q: What does blameless mean in a postmortem?
cards.a: Focusing on what the system allowed, not who made the mistake.

concepts.s: Every dataset needs a named owner and an escalation path, because tables without owners are where stale and broken data accumulates.

x.b:
• An owner (a team, with a named contact) is accountable for a dataset's correctness, freshness, and changes.
  • Ownership is recorded where people look: catalog entries, table properties, or the dbt meta block.
  • Consumers know where to report problems and what response time to expect.

• Alerts route to the owning team, not to one shared channel nobody watches.
  • Every alert links to a runbook: what it means, how to check it, how to fix or escalate it.
  • Separate pages (urgent, act now) from tickets (fix this week). Too many pages trains people to ignore them.

Ownership is usually unclear at boundaries: the source system team says "the data left our database correctly," and the BI team says "we just display it." Make ownership of each handoff explicit, often through a data contract. Periodically list datasets with no owner or no queries, then assign or retire them.

cards.q: Where should dataset ownership be recorded?
cards.a: Where people look: catalog entries, table properties, or the dbt meta block.

cards.q: What should every alert link to?
cards.a: A runbook explaining what it means, how to check it, and how to fix or escalate it.

cards.q: Why separate pages from tickets?
cards.a: Too many pages trains people to ignore them; pages are urgent, tickets are fix-this-week.

cards.q: How do you make ownership explicit at system handoffs?
cards.a: Often through a data contract.

concepts.s: Most bad numbers trace back to a small set of these patterns, so start a diagnosis by matching the symptom to its usual causes.

x.b:
• A retry re-ran an append job (idempotent writes).
  • A join to a finer-grain table fanned out rows (grain).
  • Duplicate CDC or streaming events with no dedup key.
  • A dimension gained duplicate current rows (SCD Type 2 bug).

• Incremental watermark skipped rows from long transactions.
  • Inner join to a dimension missing new members (late-arriving dimension, no Unknown member).
  • Streaming watermark dropping late events.
  • Records diverted to a DLQ nobody is watching.

• Late-arriving facts were reprocessed in the lookback window.
  • A fact joins dimensions on is_current instead of point in time.
  • A backfill rebuilt history with new logic.

• Small files accumulated (needs compaction).
  • A new hot key or NULL flood caused skew.
  • Data growth pushed a broadcast past its threshold or caused spill.
  • A filter change broke partition pruning or pushdown.

x.t: Dashboard looks fine but is stale
x.b:
• Job succeeded with zero new rows (freshness measured on job status, not data).
  • An upstream table is late; lineage shows which one.

cards.q: Name likely causes of a total doubling overnight.
cards.a: A retried append job, join fan-out to a finer grain, duplicate CDC or streaming events with no dedup key, or duplicate current rows in an SCD Type 2 dimension.

cards.q: Name likely causes of totals quietly dropping.
cards.a: A watermark skipping long-transaction rows, an inner join missing new dimension members, a streaming watermark dropping late events, or records in an unwatched DLQ.

cards.q: Why might last month's number change?
cards.a: Late facts reprocessed in the lookback window, a fact joining dimensions on is_current, or a backfill with new logic.

cards.q: Name likely causes of a job suddenly running much slower.
cards.a: Accumulated small files, new skew from a hot key or NULL flood, a broadcast past its threshold or spill, or broken partition pruning or pushdown.

cards.q: What explains a dashboard that looks fine but is stale?
cards.a: A job succeeded with zero new rows because freshness was measured on job status, or an upstream table is late.
